New York Judge Denies Novig's Injunction Bid, Rules Its Sports Contracts Are Gambling

Published November 12, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

A federal judge in the Southern District of New York has denied prediction-market platform Novig's bid for a preliminary injunction that would have blocked New York's gambling regulators from enforcing state law against it, ruling in a Tuesday opinion that Novig's sports event contracts are sports betting rather than financial swaps.

What the lawsuit was about

Novig's parent entity, Ludlow Exchange, LLC, sued New York Attorney General Letitia James and officials of the New York State Gaming Commission on August 5, after the CFTC designated it a federally regulated contract market in June and it began offering sports event contracts — including point spreads, player props, and parlays — to New York customers in August. Novig argued that the federal Commodity Exchange Act preempts New York's gambling and sports-betting laws, saying the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction because the contracts qualify as swaps.

The ruling

U.S. District Judge Colleen McMahon rejected that argument in a 35-page opinion, concluding the contracts don't meet the legal definition of a swap under the Commodity Exchange Act because sporting outcomes, while a qualifying "event or contingency," lack the financial, economic, or commercial consequence the statute requires. "The Court is not required to disregard common sense," McMahon wrote, according to Casino.org — "Novig's sports event contracts are sports betting." The ruling also found that even if the contracts were swaps, federal law wouldn't automatically override New York's authority to regulate gambling within the state.

The decision is limited to the preliminary injunction; it isn't a final ruling in the underlying case. Per reporting from The Block, New York can now require Novig to either obtain a state gambling license or stop listing and trading sports event contracts for state residents, though the ruling doesn't force an immediate shutdown. Novig previously held a Colorado sports betting license, which it gave up when it moved to its current exchange model.

Why it matters

This is the latest in a string of federal rulings on whether sports-outcome prediction markets can bypass state gambling law by operating as CFTC-regulated exchanges — a question already playing out in disputes involving Kalshi, Polymarket, and other platforms in multiple states. Sports-betting attorney Daniel Wallach noted that federal courts within the Second Circuit have now issued ten rulings on sports prediction-market litigation, with all of them favoring the states. For bettors, the practical effect is that prediction-market sports contracts remain in a legally contested position in New York and several other states, meaning availability and legal status can keep shifting even for platforms that are operating today.

Sources

  • Casino.org — "Judge Rules Novig's Sports Contracts Are Gambling, Not Financial Swaps"
